USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Finalize the Phase One agreement and hold off on the December 15 List 4B tariff hike (~$160B of consumer goods) to lock in the concessions China has already committed to on paper — roughly $40–50B in annual US agricultural purchases plus IP and currency terms. Do not escalate by letting the Dec 15 duties go into force; the deal is on the doorstep (reportedly the administration is already laying groundwork to delay it) and seizing it converts our hardline leverage into a signed win before the holiday season and the 2020 election. Pair this with continued deputy-level talks to get the text on paper.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate, not existential. The tariff war has produced a material but contained drag — industrial production is roughly flat to slightly negative and the farm belt remains exposed to Chinese retaliation (neither side wants the $156–160B consumer-goods tranche to go live because it hits US shoppers on phones, laptops and toys for the first time). Yet the US economy is fundamentally sound: consumer sentiment has rebounded to 99.3, the Fed has already eased the fed funds rate from 2.40% to 1.55%, credit spreads are tightening, and the broad dollar is steady — so there is no recession spiral. The US holds the initiative: China agreed in principle (Oct 11) to large farm purchases and IP/currency concessions, and the Oct tariff hike on $250B was canceled. On the action side, letting the Dec 15 consumer-goods tariff take effect would raise costs on US consumers during the holidays, likely trigger renewed Chinese retaliation against US agriculture, and endanger the in-principle deal — a self-inflicted political and economic wound amid impeachment. A moderate de-escalation — delaying Dec 15 in exchange for a signed Phase One — is the right instrument: it salvages our leverage as a permanent, written concession rather than burning it on a counterproductive hike. This timing makes moderate rollback (partial_rollback) appropriate; full rollback would be premature since the text is not yet signed.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Do not escalate. Stay the course toward finalizing a Phase One deal and, most urgently, secure a postponement/settlement of the December 15 tariff on ~$156B of consumer electronics before it bites. Trade concrete but bounded purchase commitments for tariff deferral/rollback, keep the Huawei/Entity List and currency-manipulator designations on the table as leverage, and avoid any retaliatory move that would hand Washington a pretext to let the Dec 15 tariff go through or walk away.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential — set at +0.4. The export economy is genuinely wounded: UNCTAD estimated US tariffs cost Chinese exporters ~$35B in H1 2019 with targeted product exports down a quarter, industrial output fell to a 17-year low in summer, and export hubs like Suzhou (exports −10% over 7 months) and Dongguan are losing orders and seeing factories relocate to Vietnam. Firm-level targeting persists (Huawei Entity List, currency-manipulator designation Aug 5), and the Dec 15 tariff on phones/laptops would finally hit mass-market consumer electronics. That justifies a clearly positive threat reading. However, it is not existential: China kept ~75% of its US exports despite the tariffs, the Phase One deal was agreed in principle on Oct 11 with China to buy $40-50B of US farm goods, and Beijing holds rare-earth and ag-purchase leverage; the US also appears unwilling to risk its own consumers/retailers by letting Dec 15 tariffs land (Bloomberg Dec 4: sides 'close' to agreeing tariff relief before Dec 15; sources say postponement is in both sides' interests). That symmetric desire for de-escalation caps the downside. Action is therefore mildly concession-leaning (+0.2, negotiate): escalating would maximise the chance the Dec 15 tariff lands and the deal collapses, exactly the worst outcome for a pressured export sector. The smart play is to keep negotiating, finalize Phase One in exchange for tariff relief, and hold firm on Huawei/currency as bargaining chips rather than escalating.
